analysis.one_liner: Lets married spouses who work for the same employer each take their own full unpaid family leave.
analysis.headline: The bill would double, from 12 to 24 weeks, the unpaid family leave a married couple working for the same employer can take together for a birth, adoption, or care of a parent, but since its December 2025 introduction it has gone no further than a Senate committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Family and Medical Leave Act, married couples who work for the same employer get a combined total of 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a birth, adoption, or care of a parent, and 26 weeks combined to care for a wounded service member. This bill deletes that combined cap so each spouse would get their own full 12 weeks, or 26 weeks for military caregiving. The bill was introduced in December 2025 and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues, where no action has been taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Married couples who both work for the same employer, and take leave for a birth or adoption, to care for a parent, or to care for a wounded service member. Instead of splitting one 12-week pot (or one 26-week pot for military caregiving), each spouse could take their own full allotment of job-protected, unpaid leave — up to 24 weeks combined for family leave, or 52 weeks combined for military caregiver leave. This affects couples in fields where spouses often work side by side, like nursing, education, agriculture, and the military-adjacent workforce. The leave is unpaid, so it protects the job rather than the paycheck.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Married couples sharing a single employer

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 102(f) of the FMLA, the provision that caps married couples who work for the same employer at 12 combined weeks of leave for a birth, adoption, or care of a parent, and 26 combined weeks for military caregiver leave.

With the cap gone, each spouse would hold their own full entitlement — meaning a couple could take up to 24 weeks combined of job-protected leave to welcome or care for a child or parent, instead of 12, and up to 52 weeks combined to care for an injured service member instead of 26.
The leave stays job-protected and health-insurance-protected under the rest of the FMLA, so a parent who takes the extra weeks cannot be fired or lose coverage for taking them.

analysis.who_pays: Employers covered by the FMLA (generally those with 50 or more employees) who have married couples on the payroll. They would face longer staffing gaps when both spouses take leave — up to double the absence for a birth, adoption, or parent-care event — and the cost of covering shifts or hiring temporary help. Workers themselves pay nothing directly, since the leave is unpaid; the financial burden of taking unpaid weeks still falls on families.

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid, so the couples most likely to need double leave time — lower-income families with a new baby or an ailing parent — are often the least able to afford taking it; the bill expands the right to take time off but provides no money to survive the time off.

Employers would absorb longer and less predictable staffing gaps when spouses at the same workplace both take leave, a cost that falls hardest on small employers near the 50-employee coverage threshold and on shift-based operations like hospitals, schools, and plants.

A doubled leave entitlement for same-employer spouses could make some employers hesitant to hire married couples into the same workplace in the first place, a risk critics of the paired-employment cap have raised because the cap's repeal removes employers' only scheduling limit on such couples.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the couples affected, the benefit is real and concrete: double the job-protected time around a birth, adoption, or a parent's illness. But the benefit is narrower than it sounds, because the leave is unpaid and only applies to married couples who share an employer and only to these specific leave reasons — leave for one's own illness or a spouse's illness is already separate under the FMLA. The cost to employers is genuine but modest and uneven. The bigger gap is that the bill expands unpaid leave without addressing whether families can afford to use it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in December 2025 and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, where it has been sitting ever since with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Senator Joni Ernst introduced the FAIR Leave Act on December 3, 2025, with Senator Maggie Hassan joining as cosponsor, making it a bipartisan two-sponsor bill.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which is the standard first step for a labor bill.
No further action appears in the record — no committee hearing, no committee vote, no Senate floor vote — as of the end of the available action history.
Because the 119th Congress runs until January 3, 2027, the bill is technically still alive, but bills that sit in committee without action for months rarely advance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. The couples who would benefit from doubled leave are waiting, and employers face no change while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Joni Ernst
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Leave Act on December 3, 2025 to remove the combined leave cap for married co-workers.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Republican sponsor (Ernst of Iowa) and one Democratic cosponsor (Hassan of New Hampshire); no one has opposed it on the record, since it has not reached a vote.

industries.industry: Covered employers (generally businesses and institutions with 50 or more employees)
industries.note: Employers with married couples on staff would face longer staffing gaps — up to twice the absence for a birth, adoption, or parent-care event — plus the cost of covering shifts or temps. The cost is modest and falls unevenly, concentrated in hospitals, schools, plants, and other workplaces where spouses commonly work side by side.
Longer employee absences at covered workplaces would modestly increase demand for temporary and substitute workers to fill in during both spouses' leave.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is a narrow, two-sponsor measure with no recorded committee activity. Most private members' bills at this stage — introduced, referred to committee, no hearing scheduled — never get a vote before the Congress ends. Unless the HELP Committee holds a hearing or a larger paid-leave package picks it up as a rider, it will likely die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027.
